Feel test Portrait One thumb Godot 4.7 · GDScript Android first Desert

88fits / design bible

Drag to run. The guns aim themselves. A portrait, third-person survivor-shooter in the Megabonk mould: clean anime-styled characters in a chunky 3D desert, a few dozen enemies on screen, level-ups that hand you three cards, and a meta that keeps you unlocking between runs.

version 0.6 date 2026-09-14 status playable, iterated from the phone engine Godot 4.7.2
Build status · 2026-09-14

Everything in this document is built in Godot 4.7.2 under game/ and verified by a parse check, 22 unit tests, a headless integration run through two bosses and every screen, silent screenshot captures, and a signed Android build. What you play today: a floating joystick with a camera bolted to the hero, the Drifter (hat, brown duster, red scarf) with video-made run cycles in eight directions, goblins, goblin runts, fire ants, spitting cacti, bull beetles and the Tumbleweed King, each spawn a different size and tint, nine weapons with nine evolutions and nine passives, a dust devil that throws enemies around, a boss countdown, a labelled pause button, Fredoka type, bold black-outline icons, a crowd of dozens that moves at a walking pace. Art is anime cel shading from Flux.2 Klein stills animated by Wan 2.2 clips on the ComfyUI server. How to run and how to get a build on the phone: docs/RUNNING.md.

Changed in v0.6
  • Structures scattered over each map: stand in the ring for three seconds and a marker fills on the ground; seven kinds, from a common healing well to the rare Uber Magnet and a travelling shop with prices set by power (section 07).
  • Hero cycles are pose-driven (a Mixamo stride through Wan 2.2 Animate, hands included), with a hit reaction in every direction; the method has its own page (section 15).
  • The two chargers, Bull Beetle and Boar, have all eight directions, so you can read where the charge is going (section 09).
  • Character icons are painted portrait badges; the Roomba is retired (section 13).
  • Shots keep their height over the ground and markings drape over it; the dead hero lies still; XP pickups say how much (sections 03, 08).
Changed in v0.5
  • A second map, Mossy Hollow: a meadow with a pond, groves, giant mushrooms, three geysers, a bee swarm and fireflies, and its own six creatures, Bramble Imp, Toadstool, Hornet, Puffball, Boar and King Toad (sections 06, 09).
  • A new default hero, Astro, an Astroneer-style explorer in a bubble helmet; the Drifter stays selectable (section 13).
  • Pickups on the ground now and then: heart, rage, sprint, shield, magnet pulse, all content, scheduled by each map (sections 07, 10).
  • The camera pulled back to 20.5 m, so the hero is about a fifth smaller and more of the field shows (section 05).
  • Hero run cycles carry 24 frames at 28 fps, creature walks 12 at 15, cut from the same video clips; strips are packed as grids (section 15).
Changed in v0.4
  • The UI was rebuilt around Survivor.io: one navy-and-gold palette, Lilita One for headers and buttons, Baloo 2 for text, outlined type over the world, and a HUD strip that takes 13% of the screen instead of a quarter (sections 03, 12).
  • Cards size themselves to their content (a new TapCard control), so icons and text never leave a button and pause rows never stretch their icons (section 12).
  • WASD and the arrow keys move the hero on a PC; the actions live in the Input Map (section 04).
  • A shortlist of free UI asset packs and the AI-painted skin route, ready for the day the look should stop being code (section 12).
  • Every capture refreshed; play setup and settings are captured too.
Changed in v0.3
  • The hold-to-run, slide-to-steer hypothesis was tested and dropped for the floating joystick the genre uses (section 04).
  • The camera is fixed, north up, bolted to the hero at 46°; the chase camera survives as an option (section 05).
  • Art direction moved from painted, through chunky Clash, to clean anime; the hero is the Drifter; sprites animate from video clips, eight directions (section 15).
  • The crowd is dozens, not hundreds, everyone walks slower, every spawn rolls size, speed and tint (sections 07, 09, 17).
  • Coyotes became goblins and goblin runts; the dust devil lifts and flings (sections 06, 09).
  • Three new weapon lines: Tumbleweed, Rattlesnake, Skull Rain with Spurs, Snake Oil and Sombrero (section 08).
  • Every weapon auto-aims and every hit shoves; a boss countdown and a PAUSE button live in the HUD; a real font and bigger UI (sections 04, 12).
  • All mock-ups replaced by captures and sprites from the build.
01

Vision & pillars

The question this project answers: does a Megabonk-style run work in portrait with one thumb? Everything below is built to get that answer fast, then to grow into a real game if the answer is yes.

The pitch in three sentences

You are a small goofy hero in a very big, very hot desert, and the desert hates you. Goblins, fire ants, and spitting cacti pour in from every side while your weapons fire on their own, so your only job is to steer through the mess, hoover up XP gems, and pick the best card every time you level up. Survive the boss, walk into the portal, and decide whether to bank your gold or push into a harder stage.

One thumb, zero menus

Every in-run action is hold, slide, or tap. If a feature needs a second finger or a button cluster, it is cut or automated.

Portrait is the point

The tall screen shows more ahead than beside. Threat comes from the front and steering is the skill. We design around it, not despite it.

Cards go brr

Vampire Survivors weapon stacking: six weapons, six passives, evolutions. Runs feel different because builds feel different.

A crowd, not a queue

Two dozen enemies on screen from minute one, sixty by the end, every one of them a little different. The screen should look like a problem you can read.

Goofy and readable

Anime-style sprites for characters (crisp line art, cel shading, flat saturated colours), real 3D for weapons, pickups, and the world. Silly on purpose, clear at a glance on a phone.

Content is data

A new weapon, passive, enemy, or shop upgrade is a new file, never new code, and it is visible and editable inside the Godot editor. See section 14.

What it is not

  • Not a parkour game. Jumps happen automatically at marked ledges and pads. There is no jump button.
  • Not an aiming game. No crosshair, no manual fire. Facing still matters for cone weapons, which gives steering a combat purpose.
  • Not a shop-between-waves game like Brotato. Progression inside a run is the starter pick and level-up cards only.
02

Reference games

Each reference is named for one thing we borrow, so later we can say "Archero-style cards" or "Megabonk-style portal" and both know exactly what is meant.

Megabonk

3D · third person · goofy

We take
Tone and humour. Stages ending in a boss and a portal. Extract-or-continue tension. Characters and items unlocked by completing in-run challenges. Permanent upgrade shop between runs. 3D pickups and weapon effects around a flat character.
We skip
Parkour, wall jumps, manual jumping, landscape framing.

Vampire Survivors

2D · the genre template

We take
Auto-firing weapons. Six weapon slots plus six passive slots. Weapon levels to 8. Evolution by pairing a max weapon with its passive. XP gems and magnet. Pick 1 of 3 on level up. Reroll, skip, and banish as meta unlocks. The pause screen that lists every item you hold.
We skip
The 30-minute timer, the arcana system, the sheer item count for now.

Archero

portrait · one thumb · mobile pacing

We take
Portrait HUD conventions. Full-screen level-up cards sized for thumbs. Chapter pacing where a run is 10 to 15 minutes with bosses on a schedule. A title screen that is one big PLAY button.
We skip
Stop-to-shoot. Rooms and doors. Equipment gacha.

Brotato

starter choice · stat transparency

We take
Picking a starting weapon before the run. A stats screen that shows every number with where it came from.
We skip
Shop between waves, discrete waves, top-down 2D.

Survivor.io

portrait Vampire Survivors

We take
Proof that the genre reads fine in portrait. Top-of-screen timer and weapon row. Evolution reveal moments. The floating joystick and the camera that never rotates: the scheme that shipped.
We skip
Monetisation layers.

The one idea without a reference, hold-to-run, slide-to-steer, was the feel test's hypothesis. It lost to the joystick on the first phone session and section 04 records why.

03

The screen

Two captures from the build show the in-run experience: the play view in Dry Gulch and the level-up choice. The HUD is a thin strip over the world, Survivor.io's proportion: everything below it belongs to the thumb.

HUD anatomy

top strip
250 px of 1920, 13% of the screen. Row one: LV badge, XP bar, stage name. Row two: kills and alive count left, the timer big in the middle, gold right. Row three: the twelve item slots. A gradient that fades into the world, no panel, every piece of text outlined so it reads over sand and sky. Tapping the strip pauses.
slots
Six weapon squares on the left, six passive circles on the right, 72 px each, a level badge in the corner that turns gold at max level. Empty slots are faint outlines. Same icon files as the cards and the pause screen.
pause
A round gold button at the right end of the strip, where Survivor.io keeps it. Two bars drawn as shapes, so no font can break it.
on the player
Health bar under the character, not in the HUD. Eyes stay on the action.
boss
BOSS IN 0:45 counts down just under the strip in the last 45 s (banner at 30, pulse under 10); the boss name and bar take the same spot while a boss is alive.
thumb zone
Everything below the strip, 86% of the screen. A faint ring appears where the thumb lands and fades after a second. Nothing is ever drawn here that needs reading.
safe areas
HUD respects the notch and gesture bar insets from the OS. Gameplay renders edge to edge.
04

Controls

The whole game is one thumb on the lower two thirds of the screen: a floating joystick, the scheme every portrait survivor game settled on (Archero, Survivor.io, Vampire Survivors mobile). Touch anywhere, the stick appears under the thumb, drag to run in that direction, lift to stop. The hold-to-run, slide-to-steer hypothesis was tried first and lost: steering a character like a car under a rotating camera fought the thumb.

The rules of the thumb

touch down
The joystick base appears under the thumb, anywhere below the top bar. No fixed position to find, no acceleration ramp: the first frame of drag already moves.
drag
Direction of the stick = direction of travel on screen (through the camera, so in the follow camera "up" is "ahead"). Dead zone 6 px. Throttle ramps to full speed at about half deflection, so a small nudge creeps through a gap and a full push sprints. The hero faces where he runs.
long drag
Past the rim the base trails the thumb, so a thumb that wandered keeps steering from where it is. Joystick size is a slider in settings (0.6 to 1.4).
lift
Stop on the spot. Standing still is a legitimate tactic. Weapons keep firing.
auto-fire
Every weapon fires on its own cooldown and every weapon aims itself: nearest, random, or a cone pointed at the nearest enemy (the shotgun family), so shots always leave towards something. The facing only decides where the held gun points when nothing is in range. Every hit pushes: each weapon carries a knockback stat (metres per second of shove on a 1 m creature; heavier creatures budge less, the boss barely).
auto-jump
Running off a marked ledge or onto a jump pad triggers a fixed arc. The player cannot fall off the map. Raised paths hold chests and shortcuts.
tap a card
Level-up and starter choice. Big targets, no drag, no confirm step.
pause
The round gold button at the right end of the HUD strip (tapping the strip works too). Full build and stats readout, options, abandon run. See section 12.
keyboard, PC only
WASD or the arrow keys move the hero exactly like a full stick push; no ring is drawn. The four actions (move_left/right/up/down) live in the project's Input Map, so they can be rebound in the editor without code. Phones never see them.
reserved
Double-tap dash and a second-thumb ability button are ideas for later. A right-thumb camera drag is only worth adding if the follow camera ever becomes the default.
What the feel test found

Turning the character was a chore, not a decision: with A and B the thumb fought the rotating camera and every dodge needed a two-step steer. The joystick makes a dodge one motion, the way the benchmark games do it, and leaves the decisions to positioning, which is where this genre keeps them.

05

Camera

v0.5

The fixed camera sits at 20.5 m (was 17) with its focus 3 m north of the hero, so he reads about a fifth smaller and the field around him is wider. The chase camera moved out the same way (19.5 m). Nothing else changed.

A fixed camera, north always up, the way Archero and Survivor.io frame the fight: the world never rotates, so the stick maps straight to the screen and the map stays learnable. It is bolted to the hero, the way Archero and Survivor.io do it: no lead, no lag, so the stick never feels like it is also steering the view. Only hits shake it. The chase camera behind the hero is kept as an option in settings ("Follow"), but it is no longer the default.

fixed (default)
Yaw locked to north, position locked to a point 2.6 m north of the hero, so he stands a little below the screen centre and sees more of what is coming. Screen shake on every hit the hero takes (and on evolutions and boss slams). The hero sprite switches between back, back-diagonal, side, front-diagonal and front views from the direction of travel, diagonals mirrored, eight directions in all.
follow (option)
Yaw follows the hero's facing with a short lag and a dead zone so turns feel weighty; the hero is seen from behind. Switch in Options at any time, even mid-run.
aspect
Keep-height projection. Every phone sees the same distance ahead. Wider phones see a bit more to the sides.
terrain
The camera rides the terrain height under the player, smoothed, so dunes and the riverbed do not bounce the view. Mesa tops raise the camera with the player.
readability
Enemies far up the screen are small. Elite and boss silhouettes are 2 to 3 times larger so they read at distance. Ranged enemies telegraph with a ground ring.
occlusion
Tall props between camera and player fade to 30% opacity. Cacti never hide the hero.
06

Environment: Dry Gulch and Mossy Hollow

v0.5 · Mossy Hollow

The second map is a meadow, built the same way (a heightmap from noise, a flat clearing, a ring wall, props as obstacles, all tunables exported), with everything the desert has replaced by a green counterpart: rolling hills instead of dunes, a pond with lily pads instead of the riverbed, a wall of pines and oaks instead of the mesa ring, groves and giant mushrooms as obstacles, mossy boulders, logs and stumps, a blue sky with cumulus and forested hills, fireflies at all hours. No tumbleweeds and no dust devil; instead three geysers that rumble (a blue ring) and then blow everything on them into the air, the hero included, every nine seconds, and a bee swarm that drifts around, homes in on the hero when he is near, and stings whoever stands in it, so a pack can be led through it. Grass, dirt, mossy rock and the sky come from tools/gen_textures_meadow.py; the trees, bush, mushroom, log and stump from tools/blender_props.py.

The first map is a golden-hour desert. It is not a plane: gentle dunes, a sunken dry riverbed, two sandstone mesas you auto-jump between, and enough oversized props that steering means something. Everything here is 3D, built low-poly in Blender and painted, and each prop is its own Godot scene.

Theme rules

time of day
Golden hour, always. Warm orange light from one side, long soft shadows baked into props, purple sky at the top. It flatters painted sprites and hides low polygon counts.
skybox
A panorama: gradient from dusk purple to orange, a big low sun, a far ring of mesa silhouettes, three lazy clouds. Optional heat shimmer near the horizon as a cheap shader. The sun is also the directional light.
ground
A 140 m heightmap terrain, not a plane. Dunes of about ±1.5 m, the riverbed 2 m lower with a cracked-earth texture, sand elsewhere with a subtle wind-ripple normal map. Two textures blended by height. Dark scorch patches break repetition.
walls
A ring of modular mesa blocks. The camera never sees past them, so the world ends without a visible edge.
props
Saguaro in three sizes, barrel cactus, prickly pear, rocks in three sizes, boulder, mesa block kit with ramp and arch, wooden signpost, bones and skulls, wrecked pickup, gas station, water tower, wind pump, campfire, tumbleweed. Cacti, rocks, and wrecks collide. Bones, tumbleweeds, and signs do not.
moving bits
Tumbleweeds roll through on the wind and bounce off things. One dust devil roams the flats and pushes player and enemies alike. The gas station sign flickers. The wind pump turns.
scale joke
The hero is small. Cacti are twice their height, the pickup is a building, the skull is a bench. Oversized props sell the goofy tone and the third-person camera.
lighting budget
One directional light, no real-time shadows on mobile, ambient from the sky colour, a fake blob shadow under every character. Campfire and portal get a single omni light each.

Blender's role

  • Props. Every prop above is modelled low-poly in Blender through its MCP, given a painted texture, and exported as GLB into res://art/props. Godot's import turns each into a scene with collision.
  • Terrain. The heightmap can be sculpted in Blender or painted in Godot. Blender wins if we want the riverbed and mesas to be hand-shaped.
  • Weapon meshes. Saw blades, the shotgun, grenades, the turret, the gem, the coin, the chest, the portal ring. Small, chunky, one texture atlas.
  • Not Blender. Characters and enemies stay 2D painted sprites. Blender never touches them.

Later themes

Two more maps once the feel test passes, each with its own skybox, ground set, prop kit, enemy skins, and boss. Candidates: a junkyard at night and a snowed-in ski lodge. A map is data plus one scene, so a theme is a content pack, not a code branch.

07

Core loop & run structure

v0.6 · structures

Nine small landmarks are scattered over every map at run start, never near the start clearing and never on top of each other, so finding them means crossing the map. Each is single use: stand inside its ring and a wedge fills on the ground over three seconds (a dark hand on its leading edge, so it reads on any ground); step out and it drains. Rarity is a weight in the content JSON.

StructureWeightWhat it does
Healing Well4Heals half of max HP.
Loot Cache360 gold, three large gems and a handful of coins.
XP Beacon3An instant level-up.
Travelling Shop2Three random items from the level-up pool with prices by power (rarity sets the base, each level held adds a third, passives a touch cheaper). Buy one with run gold and the stall packs up.
War Drum2+50% might and +25% area for 30 s.
Dice Shrine2One of: full heal, 150 gold, a level-up, or an ambush of the map's swarmers with a chest as consolation.
Uber Magnet1Every gem and coin on the ground comes home. Once.

Each structure is a folder under content/structures/ (effect kind, numbers, weight, colour, which Blender prop); a map's timeline says how many and how far apart. New kinds need a folder and, for a new effect, one more branch in Game.use_structure.

v0.5 · pickups

Every 55 to 95 seconds (the first after 50) a pickup appears a short run from the hero and waits twenty seconds, blinking at the end: a Heart (30% of max HP), Rage (+50% might for 20 s), Sprint (+40% speed, faster cooldowns, 15 s), a Shield (no damage for 6 s, the hero tinted blue) or a Magnet Pulse (every gem on the map comes home). They are never pulled by the magnet: you walk to them, through whatever is in the way. Hearts are the common one; the run stays hard because they are rare, short and somewhere else. Each is a folder under content/pickups/ and each map's timeline says which ones it offers and how often.

A run is 15 minutes in three 5-minute stages. It opens with a starter weapon pick. Each stage ends with a boss and a portal. Walk through to bank your gold with a bonus, or stay and face a harder stage. Death also ends the run and keeps what you earned.

Run rules

starter pick
Before the timer starts, three weapon cards. See section 11. The chosen weapon goes into slot 1 at level 1.
length
15 minutes for a full clear, benchmarked on Archero's early chapters and Survivor.io stages. Short enough for a bus ride, long enough for a build to come online.
stages
Three per map. The stage timer drives the wave director. Each stage raises the difficulty multiplier and the live cap and swaps in nastier variants.
boss
At the end of every stage, on the flats. Big silhouette, three telegraphed attacks, drops a chest that can trigger an evolution, exactly like Vampire Survivors chests. Regular spawning slows to a trickle while the boss lives.
portal
Appears where the boss dies. Extract banks gold at ×1.25 and ends the run. Continue starts the next stage. After stage 3, an endless mode continues with the multiplier climbing every minute.
death
Ends the run. All gold collected is kept at ×1.0. A revive is a meta unlock, one per run.
spawning
Continuous, not discrete waves. A live cap grows with time. When the cap has room, the director spawns from the current roster on the ring outside view, in bursts of 5 to 20 so groups arrive as groups.
chests
Drop from elites and bosses and sit on the mesas. A chest levels up an owned item, or evolves one if the recipe is met.
08

Weapons, passives & evolutions

v0.6.1 · poison

Poison is a debuff creatures can carry: they turn bright green and take a tick of damage every two seconds, with a green-white flicker and a puff so it is never quiet, and only a nudge of knockback. A poisoned creature keeps one entry per item: the same item hitting again resets the clock instead of stacking, a different poison item adds its own. Levelling a poison item raises its tick damage and, at a couple of levels, adds a stack; never the speed. Three items use it: the Rattlesnake is a poisoning orbit (little bite, ten seconds of venom), Skull Rain is a poison bomb that leaves a cloud of green smoke where it lands and aims for the thickest crowd of healthy creatures, and the new Poison Dart is a hovering dart that pricks the nearest healthy creature; its passive Venom raises every poison's tick, and its evolution Plague Volley throws three. The Peashooter's icon now shows its pea-pod companion. The travelling shop's prices came down to what a run actually earns (a new common item costs about a dozen gold), and it has a close button as well as Leave.

v0.5.1 · two fixes

Lobbed shots fly through the crowd. Skull Rain, Lob Grenade and their bomblets used to count as a hit on the first enemy they grazed in flight, which killed one goblin and swallowed the explosion. Arcing projectiles now ignore contact and only ever explode where they land. The Peashooter has a body. A flying pea pod with leaf wings and a face circles the hero (radius, height, speed and bob are data in params.familiar) and the peas leave its mouth; Bullet Hose grows it and gilds the leaves. Any weapon visual can carry a Familiar node the same way a forward weapon carries a Held gun.

Pure Vampire Survivors: six weapon slots, six passive slots, every item levels to 8, and a maxed weapon plus its paired passive evolves at a boss chest. The feel-test roster is six of each. Every weapon is a 3D object in the world, because saw blades, grenades, and turrets look right in 3D and a sprite of them would not.

Evolutions

A weapon at level 8 with its paired passive at level 1 or more evolves when the player opens a boss or elite chest. The evolved form replaces the weapon, gets a gold-trimmed mesh, and cannot level further. Six recipes, one per weapon:

RecipeBecomesWhat changes
Peashooter + MultishotBullet HoseContinuous stream, pierces 3, no cooldown gaps.
Boomstick + MightDoomstickDouble barrel, twice the pellets, knockback wave.
Orbit Saws + ReachSaw HaloSolid spinning ring mesh, permanent, damages everything it touches.
Lob Grenade + HasteCluster BombSplits into 6 bomblets on impact.
Zap Beam + ConductorStorm CloudA cloud mesh follows the player and strikes constantly.
Turret Buddy + MagnetTurret FamilyTurrets pull gems to you and never expire.

Level-up cards

  • Pool. Weapons not yet owned while a weapon slot is free, plus any owned weapon or passive below max level. Nothing outside the pool can appear.
  • Three cards. Luck adds a chance of a fourth. Rarity weights favour upgrades to items you already own so builds converge.
  • Reroll, skip, banish. Per-run charges bought in the shop. Skip pays a little gold so it is never a dead choice. Banish removes an item from this run's pool.
  • Card text is generated from data. The description is built from the item's effect list, so a new item never needs hand-written card copy unless we want flavour. The same generator feeds the pause screen.

Stats every effect can touch

Player stats: max_hp, armor, regen, move_speed, might, cooldown, area, projectile_speed, duration, amount, magnet, luck, greed, revives. Weapon stats: damage, cooldown, amount, pierce, area, speed, duration, knockback, chains. Any effect names a stat by string, so adding a stat is adding a key to a list, and the pause screen lists whatever keys exist.

09

Enemies & waves

v0.6 · chargers in eight directions

A charger's wind-up only warns you if you can see where it points. The Bull Beetle and the Boar now carry side, back-diagonal and front-diagonal sets besides front and back (stills edited from the front painting, a walk clip each), and while winding up or charging they face their charge direction rather than their drift. Any creature gets this by setting "directions": 8 in its JSON.

v0.5 · the meadow's creatures

Mossy Hollow uses the same four archetypes and the same boss brain with a new cast, all data in content/enemies and content/bosses: the Bramble Imp (walker, packs of three, a thorn for a dagger), the Toadstool (a slower, tougher walker from the second minute), the Hornet (swarmer, fast, eight at a time), the Puffball (spitter, keeps its distance and coughs spore clouds) and the Boar (brute, winds up and charges). King Toad is the boss: a leap along a telegraphed line, a ring of imps, and a slam. Every spawn still rolls size, speed and tint.

Four archetypes, elites, and a boss, each a data file that picks a brain, a sprite set, stats, and a drop table. Dry Gulch gives each archetype a desert skin. Two dozen are alive from the first minute and sixty by the end (the engine still handles hundreds), so every enemy is cheap: a billboard in a MultiMesh, a position in an array, and a brain that is a few lines of steering.

Dry Gulch enemyArchetype · brainRoleRead at a glance
Goblinfrom 0:00Walker · chaseThe crowd. Slow, medium HP, contact damage. Packs of 3. Every spawn rolls its size (±12%), speed (±12%) and a tint from a palette; 8% come out as specials: bigger, tougher, red-tinted, worth more XP.Sandy blob with pointed ears and a dopey tongue.
Goblin Runtfrom 0:30Walker · chaseSmaller, faster, weaker, packs of 4. Same variance rolls. Keeps the walkers from being one silhouette.Scrawny goblin in a torn rag with a rusty dagger
Fire Antfrom 1:00Swarmer · flock + chaseTiny, fast, dies to anything, comes in forty. Punishes standing still.Red specks with legs. A red tide on screen.
Spit Cactusfrom 2:30Spitter · kite at rangeShuffles to keep distance, lobs a slow green glob with a ground-ring telegraph. Forces movement.Tall green cactus with a mouth. Only cactus that walks.
Bull Beetlefrom 4:00Brute · chase + chargeTank. Winds up a charge with a red line. Big gem drop.Dark brown, twice the size, one big horn.
Eliteevery 90 s from 3:30any · base brainAny archetype with a modifier: shielded speedy splitter explosive. Always drops a chest.Glowing outline, 1.5× size, name tag.
The Tumbleweed Kingboss · 5:00 · 10:00 · 15:00boss · scriptedRolling charge with a telegraph line, spawns a ring of tumbleweeds, bounce slam with a shockwave ring. HP bar under the top band.A tumbleweed the size of the pickup, wearing a crown.

Pacing and variance. Everyone moves slower than the first build (player 3.6 m/s, walkers 1.8 m/s) and there are far fewer bodies, so each one has to earn its place: the variance block on an enemy rolls size, speed and tint per spawn and promotes a few to specials. The Goblin Runt (smaller, faster, weaker, packs of 4) joins the roster at 0:30 so the walkers are never one silhouette. Every kill is worth about three times the XP it was, so the level curve is unchanged.

Wave director

  • Live cap. Starts at 100 enemies and grows by about 10 per minute to 250 at minute 15. Swarm rings temporarily ignore the cap up to a hard limit of 300.
  • Roster. The timeline says which archetypes are eligible at a given time and with what weights. The director rolls from that roster whenever the cap has room, spawning in bursts so packs arrive together.
  • Scaling. Enemy HP and damage scale with elapsed time, then jump with the stage multiplier. Speed never scales, so dodging stays learnable.
  • Scripted events. Elite spawns, swarm rings, and bosses are timestamped entries. Events can also be conditional, for example "if player level under 10 at 5:00, delay boss by 30 s".
  • Culling. Enemies more than 30 m behind the player are teleported back onto the spawn ring ahead. Nothing is wasted, and the pressure stays in front.
  • Crowd behaviour. Separation steering on a spatial grid so sixty goblins flow around cacti and each other instead of stacking into one sprite.
10

XP & levelling

Enemies drop gems, the player walks over them, the bar fills, three cards appear. The target cadence is a level-up every 20 to 30 seconds early and every 40 to 60 seconds late, landing around level 35 to 40 by minute 15.

XP table, levels 1 to 40
gems
Small (1 xp), medium (5), large (25). 3D gem meshes that spin. Drop table per enemy. Elites and beetles drop large.
magnet
Base pickup radius about 1.5 m. Gems inside it fly to the player. Magnet passive and pickups raise it.
gem merging
When more than 300 gems sit on the ground, the oldest merge into one bigger gem, the Vampire Survivors trick that keeps performance flat with a hundred kills a minute.
vacuum pickup
A rare drop that collects every gem on the map. The best feeling in the genre. Keep it.
gold
Separate from XP. 3D coins drop rarely, chests drop lots, and greed scales it. Gold is the meta currency and never spent inside a run.
11

Run start & first play

The player starts every run with no weapon and picks one. That first choice is the run's opening move, and on the very first run it doubles as the tutorial.

The starter pick, every run

when
Immediately after GO, before the timer starts. The arena is visible behind the cards, empty, so the player sees where they are.
what
Three weapon cards from the unlocked weapon pool. No reroll, no skip. The chosen weapon enters slot 1 at level 1. Reference: Brotato's starting weapon choice.
character bias
Each character has a favourite weapon that is always one of the three and gets a bonus when chosen. Characters do not lock you into it.
why
It gives a decision before the first level-up, it makes characters flavour rather than a fixed opener, and it teaches the weapon list one card at a time.

The very first run

  1. Title screen. One big PLAY. Shop, collection, and settings are visible but quiet. No character or map select on the first run: the Drifter and Dry Gulch are preselected.
  2. Starter pick, fixed. The first offer is always Peashooter, Boomstick, and Orbit Saws, because the three teach the three targeting styles: nearest, forward, orbit. Each card carries one extra line on this run only, for example "Boomstick fires where you face, so steering aims it."
  3. Touch and drag. A hint panel says "TOUCH and DRAG anywhere below to move", then "Drag in any direction. Lift to stop." once the hero has moved 5 m and pushed the stick properly. Goblins do not spawn until the player has moved.
  4. Slide to steer. The ring grows left-right arrows: "slide to steer". Cleared by the first turn of more than 45°.
  5. Walk over gems. The first kill drops a gem with a small arrow above it. Cleared on pickup.
  6. Level up. The first card screen shows a one-line explainer per card type, weapon versus passive, and points at the HUD rows where they will appear.
  7. Pause exists. At 1:30, a 2-second toast: "tap the top bar any time to pause and see your build". Nothing else interrupts the run again.
  8. First results. The results screen explains gold in one sentence and the Shop button pulses once.

Every hint is skippable by tapping, appears once, and can be reset from settings. Total tutorial text is under 60 words. The run itself is the tutorial.

12

Menus & pause

Four screens outside the run and one inside it. The one inside it matters most: at any moment the player can pause and read exactly what every weapon, passive, and stat is doing, in words and numbers, not icons.

Look. Survivor.io is the target, and the whole look is one small file, ui/UiKit.gd. Navy panels with a lighter blue rim, one gold for the thing to press, purple for XP and passives, green for good news, red for danger. Headers, numbers and buttons are set in Lilita One, body text in Baloo 2 (both OFL, in ui/fonts); anything over the world gets a dark outline. Buttons carry a soft shadow and a darker bottom edge so they read as physical; primary buttons are white on gold with a brown rim. Sizes: HUD slots 72 px, level-up card icons 150, character cards 128, collection 100, pause rows 90.

Cards that cannot overflow. Every tappable card is a TapCard: a panel that sizes itself to its content (icon left, text column right, generous padding) and fires pressed once per tap, on touch or mouse, giving the tap up when the list starts scrolling. It replaced buttons with an anchored row inside, which clipped long quest text and stretched icons to the row height. Icons are always square and mouse-transparent, so a tap on the picture is a tap on the card.

UI kit

BGBG2BG3LINEACCENTXPGOODDANGERINFO

Everything above is drawn by code (StyleBoxFlat), which is why it stays coherent: one palette, two fonts, one factory for every box. When the look should become painted art, two routes are ready, and neither needs the layout code to change, because Godot's StyleBoxTexture stretches a painted button or panel by its nine slices.

free packs
Kenney UI Pack 2.0 (430 files, CC0), its Adventure (130, CC0) and RPG expansion (85, CC0) variants, Fantasy UI Borders (140 nine-slice frames, CC0) and Game Icons (105, CC0): the safest set, public domain, PNG plus vector. game-icons.net: 4180 flat game icons, SVG and PNG, recolourable, CC BY 3.0 (credit in the settings screen). Wenrexa: nine free casual and sci-fi UI kits (windows, panels, buttons, bars) in PNG and PSD. Casual UI Lab cartoon RPG pack (50+ elements, pay what you want, commercial use allowed) and SunGraphica casual mobile kit (20 screens, 260 icons, free demo, $3 full) are the closest to the Survivor.io look. HC Game Studios casual UI #2 is the polished paid option ($5, 70 buttons in five colours, PSD). Browse more at itch.io free GUI assets (filter CC0 on the left).
AI-painted skin
tools/gen_ui.py asks the same Flux.2 Klein server that paints the sprites for one sheet of parts on a magenta screen (six buttons, two panels, eight slot frames, three bars), keys it, cuts it into parts and writes ui/skin/skin.json with a nine-slice margin per part. The cutting is tested; the painting waits for the ComfyUI server, which was down when this pass shipped. A Godot theme built from those parts is a one-file change in UiKit.
what stays code
Layout, sizes, motion and the palette. Painted parts only replace the boxes.

Motion. Nothing appears, everything arrives: overlays fade in while their panel slides up 40 px, the three level-up cards stagger in, the portal dialog pops, toasts and the boss bar scale in, every button squashes while held, the picked card punches before the screen closes, hub lists stagger their rows, and every scene change cross-fades through black (ui/UiFx.gd, all tweens, all under 0.3 s so the thumb never waits).

Pause screen, all three tabs

build
Every weapon and passive held, expandable. Each shows: icon, name, level, plain-language description, live numbers for every stat it has, damage dealt and kills this run, what the next level adds, and evolution status with the missing piece named.
stats
Every player stat as a row with its full breakdown: base, character trait, shop tiers, passives, and total. No stat is hidden. The table below is what a row looks like.
options
Camera mode, joystick size, screen shake, sound and music volume (gold sliders), reset hints, debug panel, abandon run.
entry
The round pause button, or a tap anywhere on the HUD strip. The game freezes instantly, including sound.

The other screens

title
PLAY, the current pick chip, Shop, Collection, Settings. Gold and best run at the top. Background is the live Dry Gulch skybox with the camera slowly drifting.
play flow
PLAY → play setup: character cards (portrait, trait, favourite weapon, quest text if locked) and map cards on one screen, each card as tall as its text → GO → starter pick → run. Two taps if you keep the last choice, because the chip remembers it.

The permanent upgrade table from section 13 as a scrolling list with big buy buttons, tier pips, and a refund-all button.

Characters

v0.6 · portraits, the Roomba retired

Every hero's icon is now a painted close-up doing something (the Drifter tips his hat, Astro gives a thumbs-up with a planet in her visor, Dad a double thumbs-up), made as an edit of the hero's own front still and set into a round badge that fills the plate. The Roomba is gone: a robot vacuum has no skeleton to drive and it never earned its place. Three heroes remain.

v0.5 · Astro

Astro is the new default: a small explorer in a puffy white-and-orange suit with a bubble helmet and a backpack, Astroneer's silhouette in the game's anime line. +12% max HP, +10% pickup radius, favourite Orbit Saws with +20% area. He has the same five painted views and eight directions as the Drifter, with 24 frames per run cycle instead of 12. Existing saves switch to him once; after that the last pick sticks.

A character is a trait plus a favourite weapon. The favourite is always in the starter offer and gets a bonus if picked, so characters flavour a run without dictating it.

14

Content is data, in Godot

The one architectural rule, plus the answer to your question: yes, content can be both a data file and something you open, see, and tweak inside the Godot editor. In Godot those are the same thing.

The rule

A new weapon, passive, evolution, enemy, elite modifier, character, shop upgrade, quest, sound, or wave timeline is a new content folder and nothing else. It appears in the game the moment the folder exists. Code changes are allowed only to add a brand-new behaviour primitive that no existing file could express, and that primitive must then be reusable by any future content.

Test for every content addition: could Garry make this in the Godot editor, without asking Claude? If not, the system is wrong, not the content.

How it looks in the editor

Godot's own resource format is the data format. A custom Resource class with exported fields shows up in the Inspector as a form: sliders for numbers, dropdowns for enums like targeting, file pickers for the icon and the visual scene, and an "Add element" button for the effect list. Each content item is a folder with three files:

FileWhat it holdsHow you edit it
boomstick.tresThe numbers: stats, level table, targeting, pairing, rarity. This is the "data".Click it, edit in the Inspector. Sliders and dropdowns, no code.
boomstick_visual.tscnWhat it looks like in the world: the shotgun mesh, the pellet tracer, the muzzle flash particle, the sounds it triggers.Open it in the 3D editor, move things, swap the mesh, tweak the particle, press play to preview.
boomstick_icon.pngThe icon used by cards, the HUD, pause, and collection.Replace the file. The registry picks it up.

Enemies follow the same shape: goblin.tres for stats, brain choice, drops and the variance block; goblin.tscn holding the sprite strip and its frame counts, drawn by the billboard shader in game and previewable from the Content dock. A map is a folder with its arena scene, its wave timeline, its skybox, and its enemy skin list.

The Content dock

A small editor plugin adds a "Content" panel to Godot. It lists every item by type with its icon, warns about missing fields, and has one button per type: New weapon, New enemy, New passive. The button duplicates a template folder, renames the id, and opens the new resource in the Inspector. A Test button launches the game with that item already equipped or that enemy already spawning, so a change is playable in ten seconds.

The same weapon as JSON

The resource can also be written as JSON for spreadsheets or for reading here. A one-way importer turns JSON into the resource.

// res://content/weapons/boomstick/boomstick.json
{
  "id": "boomstick", "name": "Boomstick", "rarity": "common",
  "icon": "boomstick_icon.png",
  "visual": "boomstick_visual.tscn",
  "behavior": "ProjectileEmitter", "targeting": "forward",
  "base": { "damage": 6, "cooldown": 1.4, "amount": 5, "spread_deg": 35, "range": 6, "pierce": 0, "knockback": 2 },
  "levels": [
    [],                                                       // lv1 = base
    [{ "stat": "amount",   "op": "add", "value": 1 }],      // lv2
    [{ "stat": "damage",   "op": "mul", "value": 0.2 }],    // lv3
    [{ "stat": "cooldown", "op": "mul", "value": -0.1 }],   // lv4
    [{ "stat": "amount",   "op": "add", "value": 2 }],      // lv5
    [{ "stat": "knockback","op": "add", "value": 2 }],      // lv6
    [{ "stat": "damage",   "op": "mul", "value": 0.3 }],    // lv7
    [{ "stat": "pierce",   "op": "add", "value": 1 }]       // lv8
  ],
  "sfx": { "fire": "w_boom_fire", "hit": "w_boom_hit" },
  "evolves_with": "might", "evolves_into": "doomstick"
}

Where the line is

data only
New weapon using an existing behaviour. New passive. New evolution. New enemy using an existing brain. New elite modifier. New character. New shop tier. New quest with an existing condition type. New wave timeline. New map layout. New sound assignment. New icon.
needs code
A behaviour that does not exist yet, such as a boomerang. A brain that does not exist yet, such as a burrower. A quest condition type that does not exist yet, such as "without taking damage". Each is built once as a reusable primitive with exported parameters.
never code
Card text, icons, balance numbers, pairing recipes, rarity, unlock conditions using existing checks, which mesh a weapon uses, which sound plays.
15

Art: 3D, sprites, icons

Clean anime. Characters are cel-shaded sprites cut from video clips of their own stills, so they move like drawings and stay the same character from every direction. Everything they touch, throw, orbit, pick up, or stand on is 3D. Icons are one bold object each with a black outline, made to read at 84 px on a phone.

What is 3D and what is a sprite

ThingMade asWhy
Player, enemies, bosses2.5D sprite camera-facing billboard pivoting on the feet, flipped for facing; the hero is drawn from behindThe look you asked for. Painted faces read better than low-poly ones.
Weapons and their effects3D mesh + particlesSaw blades on a tilted orbit, a grenade on a real arc, a turret that turns its head. Sprites of these would look flat and wrong from a high camera.
Pickups: gems, coins, chests, vacuum3D mesh spinningCheap, readable from any angle, hundreds on screen through a MultiMesh.
Terrain, props, skybox3D low-poly, painted texturesThe world is 3D by definition. Props come from Blender.
Telegraphs: charge lines, spit rings, boss shockwaves3D decals on the groundThey must hug dunes and mesa edges.
Icons, cards, HUD, menus2DScreen-space UI.
Shadows under characters3D blob decalGrounds a flat sprite in a 3D world. The single most important trick for 2.5D.

The player's sprite never holds a weapon. Weapons float at marker points around the character: a hip point for the shotgun, a ring for the saws, a shoulder point for the storm cloud. That keeps the sprite one image per pose and lets any weapon pair with any character.

Sprite animation set, in from M1

v0.5.2 · pose-driven cycles

The free video clip left the stride count to the model, and the silhouette cutter could not tell a left step from a right one in the front, back and side views, so cycles came out doubled or halved. Hero cycles are now driven: a Mixamo run stride is rendered as an OpenPose skeleton from each of the five game views (tools/pose_driver.py, Blender), and Wan 2.2 Animate moves the painted still along it. Every driver frame is a sprite frame, so all five views share one 24-frame stride and loop by construction; a clip takes about a minute. Astro was repainted at the same time: a slim, feminine figure and an opaque mirrored visor with no face behind it, held through the animation with a negative prompt carried in the character JSON (anim_hint, anim_negative).

v0.5 · smoother cycles, grid strips

A run cycle now keeps 24 frames of the video clip and plays them at 28 fps (creatures: 12 at 15), the same stride length as before with twice the temporal resolution; the frame rate travels in the content JSON as fps. A hero strip is therefore 143 cells of 256 px, so artkit.pack_strip packs strips as a grid (rows of at most 16k px, strip_cols in the JSON) and both billboard shaders read the grid. Nothing else in the pipeline changed: five stills, five clips, one cut each.

Frames are few and the code does the rest. Every character gets the same named animations, so the animation system does not care which sprite sheet is loaded.

AnimationFramesRatePlayerEnemyBossTrigger
idle4 / 44 fpsbreathebreathe or twitchbreathenot moving
run12 / 814 / 10 fpstwelve frames cut from one full stride of a five-second clip of the still running in place, per view (five views, diagonals mirrored)eight frames from a clip, front and back (run_b while walking away from the camera)same as enemiesmoving
turn0—dropped: the hero leans into turns instead (shader roll)———
attack26 fps—lean back, then lunge or spitone pair per attack, three attacksbrain says attack
hit1—wincewincewincetook damage, 0.1 s
die1—knocked flateyes-crossed pose2-frame crumbleHP zero, then pop
cheer1—arms up——extract, results

Procedural layer on top, no frames needed: bob while moving, tilt into turns, scale-pop on spawn, squash on hit with a white flash, wobble when stunned, fade and shrink on death, and a shadow that stretches with the jump. These come from the shader and a few lines of code, so a two-frame coyote still looks alive. Frame sizes: 256 px for player and bosses, 128 to 192 px for enemies (from frame_px, bigger creatures get bigger cells). The hero's four run frames are rendered strides seen from behind, not derived.

Placeholder sprites for the feel test: generated in one batch on your AI server from a single prompt template, one enemy family per prompt, two frames each by asking for "pose A" and "pose B" of the same character. No consistency pass, no cleanup beyond background removal. Good enough to show the system moving, replaced wholesale at M4.

Icons

Every content item carries an icon, and the field is required. The registry shows a generated fallback tile with the item's initial if the file is missing, so a missing icon never blocks play, and the Content dock flags it.

spec
256 × 256 PNG with alpha. One silhouette, thick dark outline, three-tone shading, no text. Readable at 22 px in the HUD row.
backplates
The UI draws the backplate, not the icon file: amber rounded square for weapons, violet circle for passives, gold starburst for evolutions, teal diamond for shop upgrades, round portrait frame for characters. So one icon works everywhere.
generation
Same prompt template as sprites with "game icon, centered, single object" added. Batch script, background removal, downscale. Placeholders first, painted pass at M4.

Direction for the painted pass

characters
Clean modern anime: crisp confident line art, cel shading with two-tone shadows and sharp highlights, flat saturated colours, appealing stylized proportions, no texture noise, plus a dark outline added in the pipeline (heavier on creatures than on the hero) so silhouettes hold on sandy ground at 100 px tall. Faces always readable. The hero has back, front and side views and shows the one that matches his direction of travel; enemies are drawn from the front. Enemies look like they want to be pet but should not be.
world
Low-poly with hand-painted textures, warm sand, oversized props. The joke is scale: the hero is tiny, the cactus is a landmark.
colour
Player warm and bright. Enemies tan, red, green, brown by archetype. Gems violet, gold amber, danger red. Never reuse an archetype colour for anything else.
facing
Player has a back view and a side view, flipped. Enemies have one front view, flipped. Bosses have front and back.

Pipeline, documented for M4

  1. Style anchor. One painted style sheet (game/art/style/style_anchor.png: knight, coyote, cactus, shotgun, stopwatch in one image) is passed as a reference image to every later render, so the whole roster shares one rendering, palette and shading. Regenerate candidates with gen_art.py --anchor, install one with --pick=N.
  2. Generate. ComfyUI on the R9700 server running Flux.2 Klein 9B (4 steps, about 20 s a render) for stills and Wan 2.2 14B image-to-video (lightx2v 4 steps, about 3 minutes a clip) for motion. tools/comfy.py builds the graphs (also exported as UI-loadable workflows in tools/comfy_workflows/); tools/gen_art.py renders one still per view (heroes: back, side, front and both diagonals; creatures: front and back, each an edit of the front so the character stays the same), then tools/animate.py makes the still run in place, finds one full stride by comparing silhouettes (symmetric views fake a half stride, so the double period wins when it matches) and cuts twelve frames of it for heroes, eight for creatures: real motion instead of guessed poses (skill: sprite-animation).
  3. Check. The local vision model grades every render (one subject, not cropped, no text, flat background, right view) and failures re-roll with a new seed up to three times; the grade is kept in <id>_ai.json. Then key the green screen, drop specks and ground shadows, lift contrast, add the outline, fit the cell. tools/dl/review/phone.png shows every sprite at its on-screen size for a readability check before anything is imported.
  4. Clean. Background removal, edge cleanup, palette snap, downscale. One script, no hand work.
  5. Pack. Sprite sheet and SpriteFrames resource generated by script into the content folder. The enemy resource just points at it.
  6. Props. Modelled in Blender through its MCP, textured with generated painted tiles, exported as GLB.
16

Sound

Cartoon western: boings, splats, and twangs, with a galloping soundtrack that adds a layer per stage. Every sound below has an id that content files reference, a trigger, and a description written as a prompt for a sound AI. Placeholders are synthesised by script so the game is never silent while we wait for the real ones.

direction
Nothing realistic. Hits are "bonk" and "splat", deaths are comedic, UI is wooden and warm. Think Saturday-morning cartoon foley over a spaghetti-western guitar.
mixing rules
Voice limits per id, so forty fire ants dying is one sound with a pitch spread. Player and UI always audible. Enemy sounds attenuate with distance from the camera. Everything ducks under the level-up sting.
placeholders
A Python script writes a short WAV for every id: blips for UI, filtered noise bursts for hits, pitch sweeps for jumps and pickups, a looped chord for music. Ugly, but correct in timing and volume, and the sound map already points at the right ids.
real sounds
Generated at M4 from the description column with a sound-effects AI, then trimmed and normalised by script. Music from a music AI with the stage layers as separate stems.

17

Tech & performance budgets

engine
Godot 4.7.2, GDScript. The build already in your Downloads. Compatibility renderer for the widest Android reach. Vulkan Mobile renderer stays an option if we need it.
targets
Android first on your test phone. iOS export later, needs a Mac for the final build. 60 fps on a mid-range phone, 30 fps floor on old ones.
enemies
Budget of 60 alive by the end of a run (25 at the start), hard cap 80 during swarm rings; the arrays and MultiMeshes are still sized for 300, so the cap is a design number, not an engine one. Enemy logic is data-oriented: positions, velocities, HP, and frame index live in packed arrays, not one node per enemy. Rendering is one MultiMeshInstance3D per enemy type, billboarded in a shared shader, with the animation frame passed as per-instance custom data.
movement
Enemies are not physics bodies. Separation steering on a spatial hash grid, updated in a fixed 30 Hz tick. Player is one CharacterBody3D against terrain and static prop colliders.
projectiles
Object pooled 3D meshes. Hit checks are sphere tests against the same grid, not physics queries. Budget 300 live projectiles.
sprites
Every sprite faces the camera fully (a quad pivoting on its feet, tilted towards the lens), so nothing is seen edge-on from the high camera. The player is one quad with the sprite_billboard shader (frame, lean, squash, flash as uniforms); enemies use the MultiMesh twin with the same maths and per-instance custom data.
3D assets
Props and weapon meshes come from Blender as GLB, imported into scenes with collision. One texture atlas for props, one for weapons and pickups.
terrain
One heightmap mesh, 140 m, with a height-blended two-texture shader. Collision from the heightmap. Mesas and ramps are separate modular meshes.
save
One JSON save file: gold, shop tiers, unlocks, quest progress, settings, best runs, hint flags. Cloud sync is out of scope.
audio
A sound map resource binds every SFX id from section 16 to a file. Voice-limited pools per id so forty fire ants dying at once is one sound, not forty.
testing
Headless runs for logic tests through gdUnit4. A debug panel in the build to spawn waves, set level, equip any item, and toggle god mode.
web export
Used only as a quick way to check portrait layout in a desktop browser. Not a shipping target.

Tooling on this machine

installed
Node 24, Python 3.10, Chrome DevTools and Playwright MCPs, context7 for Godot docs.
downloaded, not installed
Godot 4.7.2 and 4.4.1 zips in Downloads. M0 unpacks 4.7.2 to a fixed path and adds it to PATH.
to install at M0
The godot-mcp server, run with npx @coding-solo/godot-mcp, pointed at the Godot binary. Android platform tools for adb. gdUnit4 inside the project. Project-local skills: godot, gdunit, sprite-pipeline, sound-pipeline.
blender
The Blender MCP is configured but its server closed on launch this session. It needs the uv tool installed and Blender running with the MCP add-on's server started before a Claude session begins. Verified at M0.
18

Milestones for the feel test

Five milestones, each answering one question on your phone. Animated sprites, 3D weapons, and a real desert greybox are in from the start, because you want to see how it looks, not only how it plays.

  1. Tooling and desert greybox

    Install Godot 4.7.2, godot-mcp, gdUnit4, adb, and the project skills. Verify Blender MCP. Then: capsule player, heightmap terrain with the riverbed and two mesa blocks, cactus and rock cubes, chase camera, the three steering variants behind a settings toggle, auto-jump gaps. Android build on your phone.

    Answers: does hold-and-slide feel good in portrait? Which variant wins? Does the terrain read?

  2. First blood

    Starter pick with Peashooter, Boomstick, and Orbit Saws as real 3D weapons. Goblins and fire ants at a few dozen alive through MultiMesh, with 2-frame placeholder sprite animations and the procedural bob, tilt, flash, and squash. 3D gems, XP bar, level-up cards with three passives. Pause screen with Build and Stats tabs.

    Answers: is auto-fire plus steering fun for five minutes with a crowd on screen? Do the sprites look alive?

  3. Full run

    All six weapons and evolutions in 3D, six passives, the Dry Gulch wave timeline to 250 alive, elites, the Tumbleweed King, portal with extract or continue, endless after stage 3. Placeholder icons for every item, procedural placeholder sound effects. Content pipeline complete: every item is a folder, the Content dock works.

    Answers: does a 15-minute run hold attention? Do builds feel different? Can you add a weapon without me?

  4. Meta and menus

    Title screen, play flow, three characters, shop with refund, quests and unlocks, collection, results screen, first-run hints, save file, debug panel, balancing CSV import.

    Answers: do you want to start another run immediately?

  5. Art and sound

    Sprite pipeline skill and painted HD sprites for the roster. Blender props textured, skybox, terrain textures. Real icons. Sound effects from a sound AI using the section 16 list, and music.

    Answers: does it look and sound like the game in your head?

19

Assumptions & open questions

Things I decided so the document could be complete. Each is a one-line change if you disagree.

  • Death ends the run. Your earlier answer read "Add 3 end a run". I took that as "a death ends a run". If you meant three lives, say so and the run rules change.
  • Starter pick happens every run, not only on the first run. Your note said "only when they first start", which I read as "at the start of a run, since they have no weapon". If you meant the first run ever, the pick becomes a one-time tutorial and characters get fixed starting weapons again.
  • Weapons are 3D, characters are sprites. The player never visibly holds a weapon in the sprite. Weapons float beside or around the character as 3D objects.
  • Enemy cap 25 to 60. The feel test found hundreds too fast and too busy to read; dozens, each a little different, is the design. The engine keeps its 300 budget so the cap can go back up in data.
  • 15-minute full clear, 5-minute stages. Archero's early chapters as the benchmark. Tunable in the wave timeline file.
  • Six weapon and six passive slots. Straight from Vampire Survivors. If the HUD row feels crowded on your phone, five and five is the fallback.
  • Placeholder sound is procedural. A script synthesises beeps, thuds, and noise bursts for every id in the list so the game is never silent. Real sounds come from a sound AI at M4.
  • Left-handed play is a settings mirror of the thumb zone and HUD, not a separate layout.
  • Game name. "88fits" is the folder name. The document uses it as a working title until you pick one.

Open questions that only more playing can answer: whether the walking pace stays right once evolutions arrive, whether specials need a mark beyond their tint and size, whether Tumbleweed and Skull Rain are as fun as they are loud, whether the dust devil should ever throw enemies at the hero, and how long endless stays interesting past minute twenty.
